summary: This informational memo recommends reclassifying RFC 1888, which dealt with OSI NSAPs and IPv6, as Historic. It says most of that document has no further value, and that one section is faulty.

plainLanguage.summary: An older document showed how to fit one kind of network address inside another. Almost nobody used it, and the one part still of interest contained two mistakes. This memo recommends that the document be marked Historic and that the useful part be fixed and resubmitted.

questions: what errors did rfc 4048 find in rfc 1888
subtitle: A short memo that recommends reclassifying RFC 1888, on OSI addresses inside IPv6, as Historic.

tldr.problem: RFC 1888 defined mappings between OSI NSAP addresses and IPv6 addresses, but one mapping was never used and the other was documented with errors.
tldr.mechanism: This memo describes the lack of use and the two errors in the IDP format description, and recommends that the IESG reclassify RFC 1888 as Historic.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1888 is obsolete. Anyone who still wants the IPv6-in-NSAP mapping is expected to correct it and resubmit it as a separate document.

today: RFC 4048 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1888. It has since been updated by RFC 4548.

sections.title: What RFC 1888 Defined
sections.content:
RFC 1888 was published as an Experimental RFC in 1996, at an early stage of IPv6 development, when it seemed important to consider using Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) addressing for IPv6. In its Sections 3 through 5 it maps certain OSI NSAP addresses inside IPv6 addresses, and shows how to carry arbitrary NSAP addresses as IPv6 destination options.

It also carried significant "health warnings" about how hard it is to route packets in the global Internet using such addresses. As far as the IETF knew, these address mappings had never been seriously used and are not supported by IPv6 implementations, and OSI deployment was not widespread enough for that to change.
sections.plainLanguage: The old document described how to carry one kind of network address inside another. It warned that this would be hard to use, and in practice nobody used it.

sections.title: Two Errors in Section 6
sections.content:
Section 6 of RFC 1888 works the other way, mapping IPv6 addresses inside OSI NSAP addresses. That had recently attracted some interest, for example to let IP addresses be expressed in an Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) context.

The memo says this section misuses the OSI Initial Domain Part (IDP) format in two ways:

  • It refers to the Internet Code Point (ICP) as a single octet, whereas it is correctly a 16-bit field.
  • It states that the first three octets are an IDP in binary format, but the OSI network service definition says the abstract syntax for the IDI is decimal digits, with a preferred binary encoding that uses a semi-octet for each digit (values 0000-1001).
sections.plainLanguage: The half that people still cared about was useful, but it wrote down the address labels incorrectly in two places: it gave one field the wrong size, and it described the wrong encoding for another.

sections.title: Recommendation and IANA Actions
sections.content:
Because one mapping was unused and the other was documented incorrectly, the memo recommends that the IESG reclassify RFC 1888 as Historic. It assumes that parties who wish to map IPv6 addresses inside OSI NSAP addresses will correct, augment and resubmit Section 6 as a separate document.

IANA has marked the IPv6 address prefix 0000 001, reserved for NSAP allocation in RFC 3513, simply as Reserved. The registry for the "OSI NSAPA Internet Code Point" implied by Section 6 is held in abeyance until a replacement for that section is approved. The memo sees no known impact on Internet security.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo asks that the old document be set aside. If anyone still needs the mapping described in the useful half, they should correct it and publish it again on its own.

references.text: Bound, J., Carpenter, B., Harrington, D., Houldsworth, J., and A. Lloyd, "OSI NSAPs and IPv6", RFC 1888, August 1996.
Hinden, R. and S. Deering, "Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) Addressing Architecture", RFC 3513, April 2003.
